column11: How does the regenerative nodule -> dysplastic nodule -> HCC sequence produce the classic arterial-enhancement/washout pattern?
column12: In cirrhosis, regenerative nodules are portal-vein supplied and are not premalignant. Dysplastic nodules are premalignant and most remain portal supplied unless high grade. With malignant transformation, neovascularity increases and the lesion acquires arterial supply, producing arterial hyperenhancement; progressed HCC then shows relative hypoenhancement on portal/delayed phases and may develop an enhancing capsule. The same vascular remodeling also explains why HCC can invade portal/hepatic veins and the IVC.

column11: Why does a THAD appear as arterial-phase hyperenhancement that disappears on portal venous imaging?
column12: A THAD is a perfusion phenomenon caused by reduced portal venous inflow to a territory, commonly from obstruction or compression of a portal vein branch. Compensatory increased arterial flow makes the involved wedge of liver transiently hyperenhancing on arterial phase. Once portal venous enhancement equilibrates, the area becomes isodense to background liver; the key interpretation pivot is that there is no true persistent mass.

column11: Why does FNH retain gadoxetate on hepatobiliary-phase MRI while hepatic adenoma generally does not?
column12: FNH is a hamartoma composed of disorganized liver tissue that includes hepatocytes and biliary ductules. Because functioning hepatocytes and biliary elements are present, FNH typically retains gadoxetate and becomes iso- or hyperintense relative to liver on hepatobiliary phase. Hepatic adenoma contains hepatocytes but lacks bile ducts, which also explains its usual paucity of HIDA uptake. This tissue-architecture difference is a major FNH-versus-adenoma discriminator.

column11: What tissue architecture explains blood-pool matching and progressive centripetal fill-in in hepatic cavernous hemangioma?
column12: Hepatic cavernous hemangioma is composed of disorganized endothelial-lined vascular spaces supplied from peripheral hepatic arterial branches. Contrast therefore enters peripheral vascular spaces first, creating discontinuous nodular peripheral enhancement, then progressively fills more central vascular spaces over time. Because the enhancing spaces contain contrast-opacified blood, their signal/attenuation tracks the blood pool across phases.

column11: How can SVC obstruction create focal arterial hyperenhancement in the left hepatic lobe without a true mass?
column12: With SVC obstruction, collateral venous pathways can route contrast-rich blood from thoracoabdominal collaterals toward the portal venous system, including pathways involving superficial epigastric/umbilical or internal mammary/inferior phrenic veins. This produces early focal enhancement, classically in the left lobe/medial segment, without mass effect. The imaging pivot is to trace the collateral pathway and confirm venous-phase normalization rather than diagnosing a hepatic tumor.

column13: A hypervascular liver mass has a central scar. What pitfall should be avoided, and what imaging check best separates FNH from fibrolamellar HCC?

Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis. Core was used only for the retrieved liver-mass sections documented in the audit block; RadPrimer supplies the differential backbone and STATdx supplies the selected image/caption set.
🔍 Summary
  • Characterize both morphology and hemodynamics across phases; the key discriminator is how a lesion behaves relative to liver and blood pool.
  • Hemangioma: blood-pool-equivalent enhancement with peripheral discontinuous nodules and progressive centripetal fill-in; small lesions may flash fill.
  • FNH: bright homogeneous arterial enhancement with near-isodensity/isointensity on portal and delayed phases; a central scar may be present.
  • Arterioportal shunts: commonly small and peripheral in cirrhotic liver, often wedge-shaped, arterial-only, and associated with early portal-branch filling.
  • THAD: peripheral wedge-shaped arterial hyperperfusion that normalizes on portal venous imaging, usually from altered portal flow.
  • HCC: typically heterogeneous arterial hyperenhancement with portal/delayed washout; evaluate for venous and biliary invasion.
  • Hypervascular metastases: multiplicity, heterogeneity, and ring enhancement favor malignancy; common primaries include neuroendocrine tumors, melanoma, and renal cell carcinoma.
  • Hepatic adenoma: usually heterogeneously hypervascular and may contain fat, necrosis, or hemorrhage; gadoxetate-delayed relative hypointensity is illustrated in the supplied inflammatory adenoma case.
  • HHT: enlarged hepatic arteries and draining veins with heterogeneous arterial-phase enhancement and early venous opacification.
  • Large regenerative nodules in Budd-Chiari can be multiple and hypervascular, with persistent portal-phase enhancement in the supplied CT/MR examples.
  • Fibrolamellar HCC: large heterogeneous mass in a young patient, often with a large central scar that may calcify.
  • Peripheral cholangiocarcinoma: may be hypervascular but delayed persistent enhancement and capsular retraction favor it over HCC.
  • Hepatic angiomyolipoma: nonfatty tissue may be hypervascular; macroscopic fat is visible in only about half of hepatic AMLs in the article.
  • Hepatic angiosarcoma can show bizarre eccentric hypervascular enhancement and multifocal liver/spleen involvement.
  • SVC obstruction can create left-lobe pseudolesional hyperenhancement through collateral pathways without a true mass.
  • Peliosis can show early globular or ring-like vascular enhancement with progressive fill-in, overlapping with hemangioma.

  • Do not equate every arterial focus in cirrhosis with HCC; transient wedge-shaped shunts that disappear on later phases are an important mimic.
  • Do not equate every central scar with FNH; fibrolamellar HCC is typically large and heterogeneous, and calcification within the scar is a major warning feature.
  • Hemangioma should track blood pool; persistent delayed enhancement denser than liver and blood vessels is not the expected hemangioma pattern.

column15: For hepatic involvement by HHT, what arterial-phase CT pattern should be recognized?

Enlarged hepatic arteries and draining veins/vascular masses with heterogeneous arterial-phase liver enhancement; early venous opacification may be present.

column15: For large regenerative nodules in Budd-Chiari, what CT/MRI behavior can mimic a hypervascular tumor?

column15: For fibrolamellar HCC, what imaging pattern should be recognized?
column16:
Large heterogeneous liver mass in a young patient without cirrhosis, classically with a fibrotic central scar; the article emphasizes calcification within a large scar.
Core: fibrotic scar is T1/T2 hypointense; capsular retraction may occur.
Recognition pivot: Young noncirrhotic patient + large heterogeneous scarred mass.

Delayed/progressive persistent enhancement; article clue: capsular retraction, which is not expected in HCC.

Broad left-lobe/medial-segment hypervascularity without mass effect, with thoracoabdominal and capsular collaterals; liver normalizes on venous phase.

column15: For peliosis hepatis, what CT enhancement pattern should be recognized?
column16:
Arterial phase: early globular/vessel-like or continuous ring enhancement; later imaging may show centrifugal or centripetal/progressive fill-in without mass effect on hepatic vessels.
Key differentiator: Hemangiomas usually show discontinuous nodular peripheral enhancement.
Recognition pivot: Vascular fill-in pattern with absent mass effect.
